comparator.name: Security Studies
comparator.academicYear: 2026–27 current prospectus and adopted OER, checked 2026-09-27
comparator.route: Ordinary 180-EC English-taught full-time BSc; 150 EC compulsory curriculum plus the programme’s 30-EC third-year elective space
comparator.sourceNotes: The binding 2026–27 prospectus provides the current component-level reconstruction and totals 60 EC in each year. Year one is 60 EC of security foundations, Syria and Fukushima case studies, three skills labs, research methods and an integrated project. Year two is 60 EC of vital interests, terrorism and counterterrorism, cyber threats, war and peacebuilding, law, economics, and quantitative and qualitative methods. Year three preserves 30 EC of genuine first-semester elective space and requires a 15-EC individual thesis, 10-EC Integrated Project 2 and 5-EC Governance of Security. The adopted OER, valid from 1 September 2026, confirms 180 EC total, 150 EC compulsory, 30 EC optional, no specialisation, full-time English delivery, and the prospectus as an integral binding source. No particular minor, internship or exchange package is inserted into the open 30 EC.
components: Genuine open space for an approved minor, electives, internship, study abroad or a combination.

routeSelection.route: Ordinary 180-EC English-taught full-time BSc; 150 EC compulsory curriculum plus the programme’s 30-EC third-year elective space
routeSelection.basis: The 2026–27 OER states that Security Studies has no specialisations. The reconstruction therefore follows the full target-named compulsory curriculum and preserves the programme’s 30-EC elective space without selecting a minor, internship or exchange destination to improve UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Security, conflict and governance
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum combines security institutions, conflict and peace, law, history, economics, extremism, data and mixed research methods; the label describes that broad centre of gravity.
alternatives.concept: A broad interdisciplinary security programme connecting political institutions, international relations, conflict and peacebuilding, criminal and international law, historical security, economics, extremism, data analysis and qualitative research. It is the closest feasible UCR response to Leiden’s multi-actor and multi-level Security Studies core.
progression: Law, politics, economics, research and data foundations precede advanced EU governance, conflict, extremism, econometrics and independent historical research. All formal prerequisites and planned-semester constraints pass.

alternatives.label: Crisis, disaster and societal resilience
alternatives.labelReason: Natural hazards, public health, climate risk, social behaviour, law, governance, data and applied partner research form a coherent crisis-preparedness and recovery route.
alternatives.concept: Concentrates on how societies anticipate, govern and recover from crises: natural hazards, climate risk, pandemic security, social behaviour, public institutions, law and conflict. Quantitative and qualitative methods plus an external-partner project support evidence-based crisis policy.
progression: Security, public-health, data and governance foundations precede hazards, conflict, law, advanced resilience, applied research and policy courses; Research Methods precedes Econometrics, and all term offerings pass.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the broad route, this schedule replaces economics, political theory, human rights, constitutional and EU law, imperial history and machine learning with epidemiology, natural hazards, climate change, sociology, psychology, sustainability governance and an external-partner resilience project.

alternatives.label: Cyber threats, data and security governance
alternatives.labelReason: Programming, algorithms, databases, AI, machine learning and deep learning are integrated with law, institutions, international relations and security research.
alternatives.concept: Studies cyber threats as a governance problem requiring technical literacy, data methods, law and political institutions. Programming, algorithms, databases, AI and machine learning are sequenced alongside international law, EU governance, conflict studies and qualitative and econometric research.
progression: Programming and mathematical foundations precede decision-making in AI, algorithms and deep learning; the law gateway precedes international, criminal and EU law, and Research Methods precedes Econometrics. Every course is offered in its assigned term.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with both earlier routes, this programme adds a sequenced technical strand in programming, mathematics, databases, algorithms, AI ethics, machine learning and deep learning while retaining law, governance, conflict and research. It differs from each by well over four courses.

candidates.label: Cyber threats, data and security governance

selection.assessment: Three evidence-backed and pairwise-distinct UCR programmes are feasible: broad security, conflict and governance; crisis, disaster and societal resilience; and cyber threats, data and security governance. Remaining rows are curricular topics, examples or outcomes rather than a fourth generator-owned direction.

blocks: Security, political institutions, conflict and history
Both introduce security as an institutional and societal problem; UCR begins from law, justice and governance.
Modern History provides political and historical context for conflict, including but not limited to Syria.
Both examine institutions and collective interests; UCR focuses on EU multi-level governance.
Both analyse conflict and peacebuilding, though UCR is a general peace-and-conflict course.
Both study extremism and responses to political violence; UCR focuses on youth resilience.
Law, crime and economics of security
Both examine legal institutions relevant to security; UCR focuses on public international law.
Both use economics to understand welfare and stability; UCR teaches international macroeconomics rather than a dedicated security-economics course.
Crisis, disaster, health and societal resilience
Both examine a disaster through risk and societal-response lenses; UCR covers natural hazards generally rather than the Fukushima case.
Both conduct applied work for an external partner; UCR’s sustainability project is not Leiden’s security-policy project.
Both analyse multi-actor governance of collective risks; UCR focuses on sustainability governance.
Programming provides technical literacy relevant to cyber threats, but does not reproduce Leiden’s interdisciplinary 10-EC Cyber Threats course.
Skills, research methods, projects and open space
Both develop academic, teamwork and professional reflection skills; Leiden’s skills lab is programme-specific.
Both introduce research design and quantitative methods.
Both develop quantitative analysis; UCR uses broader data-science tools.
Both teach qualitative research design and interpretation.
Leiden’s compulsory 10-EC first integrated project is not an ordinary UCR course.
The compulsory individual 15-EC Security Studies thesis cannot be counted as an ordinary UCR course or UCR’s optional research element.
The genuine 30-EC elective space remains student-selected and is not treated as fixed security content.

notes.text: Leiden’s BSc has a tightly integrated sequence of programme-specific skills labs, case studies, two integrated projects and a compulsory Security Studies thesis. UCR can build three coherent security-related schedules, but it does not reproduce those named components or the same dedicated 150-EC Security Studies core; pairings show substantive overlap rather than transfer equivalence.
